description: For people who want progress our journey through the stars.
summary:
Lunar mission planning is not held back by a lack of data, but by the challenge of turning that data into decisions.

Selenix is a browser-based, terrain-aware mission-planning and decision-support platform developed to help lunar mission planners assess how changes to variables such as landing site or date affect mission conditions, requirements & feasibility.

It brings together existing scientific resources to evaluate lunar conditions under different variables for scenario comparison: planners can assess alternative landing locations and dates side by side against the same user-defined mission requirements, identify trade-offs and understand where a scenario falls short and why.

Key results are traceable to their source data, calculation methods, assumptions and validation status, making the analysis transparent rather than a black box.

Selenix aims to reduce repetitive data navigation and reassessment, giving engineering teams more time to evaluate alternatives and make better, more informed decisions earlier on in the lunar mission planning workflow conserving planners' time and energy.

(Current stage: It is a working browser-based MVP and decision-support prototype, not a certification of landing safety or overall mission feasibility.)
details:
SELENIX — Project Description

1. What does it do and how does it work?

Selenix is a browser-based, terrain-aware decision-support platform for lunar south-pole mission planning. It addresses a recurring challenge: when a proposed landing site or date changes, mission teams need to reassess how those changes affect environmental conditions and whether the revised plan still meets its requirements.

Its central function is scenario comparison. Selenix brings alternative landing-site and date configurations into one workspace, evaluates them using consistent scientific methods and engineering assumptions, and compares their performance against the same mission objectives and requirements. The current prototype supports up to three scenarios side by side.

Each scenario is defined by its landing location, landing date and time, mission duration, relevant engineering assumptions and requirements.

The platform then compares:

  • Sun and Earth visibility throughout the mission.
  • The duration and timing of visibility windows and interruptions.
  • The longest periods without sunlight or direct-to-Earth visibility.
  • Changes in mission requirement verdicts.
  • The operational implications and trade-offs between alternatives.

For example, delaying a landing by 21 days at the same site can significantly reduce both Sun and Earth visibility. Moving to another site may restore sunlight but result in no direct-to-Earth visibility during the evaluated period. Selenix makes these differences visible on a shared mission-elapsed-time timeline, helping planners understand what each alternative gains and gives up. It does not automatically select a preferred scenario; the decision remains with the mission team.

Scientific analysis and requirement evaluation

The scientific foundation combines existing datasets, tools and interfaces such as SPICE, (LRO) LOLA elevation models etc. Selenix calculates the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth relative to a selected lunar site, then evaluates whether surrounding terrain obstructs those directions. Earth visibility also accounts for a minimum antenna elevation.

Visibility is classified into three states: visible, uncertain and obstructed. This distinction helps prevent results close to a terrain horizon from being presented as certain.

The platform evaluates the resulting conditions against explicit, editable mission requirements. The current prototype includes five principal checks:

These thresholds are demonstration defaults, not universal lunar mission standards. Planners can adjust them to reflect different mission architectures. Each requirement returns a verdict: meets, needs review, does not meet or unknown. The platform also explains the evidence and conditions behind each result.

A mission timeline shows when visibility conditions change, including individual windows, their durations and the longest interruptions.

A rule-based mission log translates significant conditions into plain-language observations, such as landing in darkness or losing direct-to-Earth geometry. These entries are based on predefined rules and calculated values, not unrestricted AI-generated conclusions.

Evidence and traceability

Every important result can be inspected through an evidence layer that identifies its source data, dataset version, inputs, calculation method, assumptions, tolerances, limitations and validation status. Results are distinguished as measured data, computed geometry, engineering estimates, user assumptions or demonstration-only information.

Uncertainty and missing information are not silently treated as favourable conditions. For example, a site without terrain data cannot be assumed to have an unobstructed horizon. Its visibility results are marked as upper bounds, and a positive terrain-dependent requirement verdict cannot be confirmed on that basis.

The current prototype also includes a simplified power and battery estimate to illustrate how sunlight availability may affect energy planning. This is explicitly labelled an engineering estimate, not a validated spacecraft power-system model.

2. What benefits does it offer?

Selenix's main benefit is making alternative mission configurations easier to assess consistently. Rather than reconstructing separate analyses whenever a landing date or location changes, planners can compare the alternatives using the same calculation methods, assumptions and requirements.

This provides several practical benefits:

  • Clearer trade-offs: Sunlight and Earth visibility can be assessed together, making it easier to identify where an alternative improves one condition while compromising another.
  • Faster reassessment: Changes to a site or date can be evaluated within the same workflow rather than manually reconnecting separate analyses.
  • Mission-focused results: Scientific measurements are connected to explicit requirements, visibility windows and potential operational implications.
  • Greater transparency: Users can inspect the evidence behind results and understand why a requirement is met, missed or flagged for review.
  • More consistent comparisons: Scenarios use common methods and tolerances, reducing the risk of comparing results produced under different assumptions.

The platform is designed primarily for lunar mission planners and mission designers, with systems, power and communications engineers as secondary users. Its interface presents the main planning information clearly while keeping technical evidence available for closer investigation.

3. What is the intended impact?

Selenix aims to make lunar mission reassessment more accessible, repeatable and evidence-based for mission planners making the process more efficient / reducing time needed to manually navigate through data to focus time, energy and resources on the decision making process.

NASA and other organisations already provide extensive lunar datasets, scientific models and specialist tools. The challenge addressed is the work required to connect these resources and repeatedly translate their outputs into mission-level decisions when planning inputs change.

By bringing these analyses into a common comparison workflow, Selenix aims to help teams identify the consequences of changes earlier, understand the compromises between alternatives and make more informed planning decisions.

The longer-term ambition is to develop the prototype into a broader mission-planning environment, with expanded terrain coverage, more detailed power and thermal models, communications link analysis and additional mission constraints.

4. What tools, coding languages or software were used?

Selenix combines established scientific datasets with custom processing and a lightweight browser application. Computationally intensive scientific processing is performed offline, while the resulting data is used by the interactive browser-based platform.

Scientific data and resources

The project uses different sources for distinct purposes. Some provide the primary inputs for calculations, while others support benchmarking, independent verification or site inspection.

Primary calculation datasets

  • NASA NAIF SPICE kernels: The primary source for planetary and lunar geometry. The project uses the DE440 planetary ephemeris, lunar orientation and reference-frame kernels, and a leap-seconds kernel. These provide the information needed to calculate the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the Moon over the evaluated period.
  • LRO LOLA elevation models: Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter digital elevation models archived through NASA's Planetary Data System. The project uses the polar products LDEM_85S_40M, LDEM_80S_80M and LDEM_75S_120M (PDS3 V2.0). These provide lunar surface elevation data used to derive terrain horizons and assess local obstruction.

Benchmarking and independent verification

  • NASA GSFC Planetary Geology, Geophysics and Geochemistry Laboratory (PGDA), Product 69: Published lunar polar illumination and Earth-visibility maps, including the AVGVISIB products. These are used to benchmark SELENIX's calculated illumination and Earth-visibility results against published reference maps.
  • JPL Horizons: An independent source of celestial geometry calculations. The project uses the Horizons API with DE441 for selected cross-checks against its primary SPICE-based calculations. Horizons is used for independent verification, not as the main calculation engine.

Mapping and site-inspection resources

  • LROC QuickMap: Lunar imagery and topographic mapping used to inspect candidate locations and verify geographic context.
  • NASA Moon Trek: Three-dimensional lunar terrain visualisation used to examine the surface and support site inspection.
  • LROC image 1408: Used as a reference for verifying the Mons Mouton location.
  • ISRO Chandrayaan-3 Shiv Shakti landing-site coordinates: Used as a lower-latitude reference location. Terrain data was not available for this reference in the current project.

Development technologies

  • Python 3, NumPy and SpiceyPy: Offline scientific processing, SPICE calculations, ephemeris generation and terrain-horizon modelling.
  • Matplotlib and Pillow: Data visualisation and image processing.
  • JavaScript, HTML and CSS: Browser-based calculation engine and user interface.
  • SVG and HTML Canvas: Charts and visual representations.
  • Node.js and Playwright: Regression testing and automated browser testing.
  • Vercel or GitHub Pages: Static deployment.

The architecture separates computationally intensive processing from the interactive interface. SPICE calculations, terrain-horizon generation and other data preparation are performed offline in Python. The resulting ephemeris tables, terrain masks and supporting data are packaged with the browser engine into a self-contained HTML application of approximately 2.2 MB.

The browser application has no runtime backend dependency and can operate offline. This approach keeps the interface lightweight while retaining the scientific data and calculations needed for scenario analysis.

5. How is the project creative?

Selenix's contribution is not the invention of new lunar datasets or celestial mechanics methods. Its creativity lies in integrating established scientific resources into a repeatable, mission-focused decision workflow. Its contribution lies in how it translates the datapoints to measurable operational decisions and maps them to specific impacts on the mission plan.

Existing resources provide important capabilities, such as celestial ephemerides, lunar topography etc. However, planners still need to connect these outputs to a particular landing location, date, mission timeline and set of requirements. When a planning input changes, the analysis may need to be revisited and compared again.

Selenix brings the stages of mission planning together through three main ideas:

  1. Compare alternatives rather than inspect them in isolation. Multiple site-and-date scenarios can be evaluated on a shared timeline, making the consequences of a change easier to identify.
  2. Evaluate Sun and Earth visibility together against terrain. This reveals trade-offs between solar availability and direct-to-Earth geometry rather than treating them as unrelated measurements.
  3. Connect results to evidence and requirements. Each important measurement and verdict can be traced to its inputs, methods, assumptions and validation status.

The platform is designed to make complex scientific analysis accessible without hiding its technical basis. It builds on existing scientific infrastructure rather than attempting to replace it - and that, is where its creativity lies. Not reinventing the wheel, but building a layer on top of it.

6. What factors did the team consider?

The team considered scientific reliability, comparability, uncertainty, usability and the limits of the available data and models.

  • Consistency between scenarios: Alternative configurations must use the same geometry, terrain methods, tolerances and assumptions for their results to be meaningfully compared.
  • Terrain accuracy and coverage: The lunar south-pole environment requires terrain-aware analysis. The available LOLA models have finite resolution and do not cover every possible site.
  • Uncertainty and missing data: Visibility close to a horizon or based on incomplete terrain information must be identified rather than presented as a definite result.
  • Mission-specific requirements: Acceptable visibility and interruption durations depend on the mission architecture. Demonstration thresholds are therefore editable and are not presented as universal standards.
  • Traceability and validation: Calculations need to be checked against independent references, and users must be able to inspect the evidence behind important results.
  • Accessibility and performance: Computationally intensive processing is performed offline so the browser interface can remain lightweight and usable without a runtime server.
  • Responsible interpretation: Geometric Earth visibility does not establish a usable communications link, and estimated battery performance does not establish full power-system feasibility.

Across 30 Sun and Earth geometry comparisons, the worst angular difference from JPL Horizons was 0.00002°. Against 45 points from NASA's published illumination maps, the median absolute difference was 0.97 percentage points for Sun illumination and 0.24 percentage points for Earth visibility. These checks support the current computational foundation but do not constitute full mission validation.

Current limitations and future development

The prototype demonstrates a defined set of scientific calculations and decision-support capabilities; it does not model the full complexity of an operational lunar mission. Its main limitations include:

  • Terrain masks are currently available for curated sites, with elevation models at 40–120 m resolution. Small obstacles, boulders and lander-scale features are not resolved.
  • The current visibility classifier uses the celestial body's centre with a tolerance band rather than a complete partial-disc model.
  • Precomputed ephemeris coverage is limited to 2026–2030, and summary metrics depend on the selected 5-, 10- or 30-minute sampling interval.
  • Earth visibility is a geometric line-of-sight assessment above an antenna elevation threshold, not a communications link budget. Relay orbits, antenna pointing and ground-station availability are not yet modelled.
  • Power and battery calculations are simplified estimates and do not yet include validated thermal, dust, degradation or heater models.
  • The platform does not yet include a complete mission-operations model covering activity dependencies, rover movement or resource conflicts.
  • The proposed time-saving benefit has not yet been measured through testing with professional mission planners.

Future development will focus on improving terrain coverage and resolution, refining uncertainty and partial-disc modelling, validating power and thermal estimates, adding communications link analysis and expanding scenario management. Structured user testing will also be needed to measure the platform's practical value.

Overall, Selenix is intended to help lunar mission teams move from analysing individual datasets to comparing mission alternatives. Its purpose is to make the consequences of changing a landing site or date clearer, more consistent and easier to trace, while leaving engineering judgement and final mission decisions with the team.
